title: The Supply Side of Social Media
abstract: We study an overlooked feature of social media: its distinctive model of content production. Unlike legacy media outlets, social media platforms do not professionally produce content ex-ante optimized to appeal to viewers; instead, they rely on large numbers of amateur users creating content in pursuit of social status, expressive satisfaction, or creative fulfillment. They then cherry-pick the pieces ex-post most appealing to viewers. We develop an equilibrium model of this process. We show that because the production scale powering platforms' cherry-picking concentrates where creators are eager to produce, creators' supply-side preferences can influence what viewers consume. Collecting new data on Instagram, TikTok, and X/Twitter, we show that most of the content in viewers' feeds is created by non-professionals who produce envy-provoking “lifestyle” and partisan political content in pursuit of social status and expressive satisfaction. To separate supply- and demand-side preferences, we experimentally manipulate viewers' feeds and pay creators to post different types of content. Piece by piece, lifestyle and partisan political content is less likely to highly engage viewers than more benign entertainment. But the satisfaction creators derive from creating such content leads it to be produced at an enormous scale. Platforms then cherry-pick the minority of such pieces viewers find more interesting or entertaining than the marginal piece of entertainment. Estimating our model using the experimental variation, we calculate that supply-side preferences account for one- to two-thirds of the prevalence of lifestyle and partisan content in viewers' feeds.
